cards.explanation: The answer is false teachers. Peter says there were false prophets among the people back then, “…just as there will be false teachers among you.” (2 Peter 2:1) Same kind of trouble, new faces, friends. And these ones don't come with a warning label.

The answer is False. Peter says the false teachers “…will secretly introduce destructive heresies…” (2 Peter 2:1). Secretly means quietly, not out in the open where everyone can see. So this one is False, friends.

The answer is the Master who bought them. Peter says they go so far as “…even denying the Master who bought them…” (2 Peter 2:1). That's not a small slip, friends. It's turning away from the very Master who bought them.
The answer is False. Peter says “Many will follow in their depravity…” (2 Peter 2:2). That's a crowd, not a handful. It's a good reason he's warning them now, friends.

The answer is truth. Peter says “Many will follow in their depravity, and because of them the way of truth will be defamed.” (2 Peter 2:2) Defamed means its name gets dragged around unfairly. Truth is the way that takes the hit, friends.

The answer is greed. Peter says “In their greed, these false teachers will exploit you with deceptive words.” (2 Peter 2:3) Greed is when someone eyes the whole cookie box and wants your share too. And the tool they use is words that deceive.

The answer is that God cast them into hell in chains of darkness. Peter says God “…cast them deep into hell, placing them in chains of darkness to be held for judgment…” (2 Peter 2:4). He did not spare the angels when they sinned. That's the first example in Peter's case, friends.

The answer is Noah. Peter says God “…preserved Noah, a preacher of righteousness, among the eight…” (2 Peter 2:5). Eight people were preserved, and Noah was one of them. Even in this second example, friends, God knew exactly who to keep.

The answer is as an example of what is coming on the ungodly. Peter says God condemned Sodom and Gomorrah, “…reducing them to ashes as an example of what is coming on the ungodly…” (2 Peter 2:6). It's the third example in his case, and Peter says what it's an example of. He doesn't add any other reason, friends.

The answer is True. Peter says Lot, the righteous man God rescued, “…was tormented in his righteous soul by the lawless deeds he saw and heard…” (2 Peter 2:8). He lived among them day after day. I think that sounds exhausting, and Peter calls it torment.

The answer is that the Lord knows how to rescue the godly and hold the unrighteous for punishment. Peter says “…the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials and to hold the unrighteous for punishment on the day of judgment.” (2 Peter 2:9) That's the whole point of all those ifs. Noah and Lot were the rescued ones. The angels were placed in chains of darkness to be held for judgment (2 Peter 2:4), and the ancient world and the cities were brought to destruction.

The answer is False. Peter says “Bold and self-willed, they are unafraid to slander glorious beings.” (2 Peter 2:10) Timid doesn't fit that description. Bold and unafraid is the picture, friends, and it's not a compliment here.

The answer is that they don't dare bring such slanderous charges. Peter says “Yet not even angels, though greater in strength and power, dare to bring such slanderous charges against them before the Lord.” (2 Peter 2:11) So even the stronger ones hold back. The false teachers don't, friends, and that's Peter's whole point.

The answer is that they do not understand them. Peter says “They blaspheme in matters they do not understand…” (2 Peter 2:12). Think of someone giving you stamping advice who has never held a stamper. I've met that guy, and he was LOUD.
The answer is False. Peter says “They consider it a pleasure to carouse in broad daylight.” (2 Peter 2:13) Broad daylight, not after dark. A pleasure, he says, and in the middle of the day, friends.

The answer is as they feast with the believers. Peter says they are “…blots and blemishes, reveling in their deception as they feast with you.” (2 Peter 2:13) They're at the feast alongside the believers. Peter names that as the very moment they revel in their deception, friends.
The answer is unstable. Peter says “they seduce the unstable.” (2 Peter 2:14) Unstable means not steady, like a cooling rack with one short leg. It's the shaky ones who get pulled along, friends.

The answer is the wages of wickedness. Peter says the false teachers have wandered off to follow “…the way of Balaam son of Beor, who loved the wages of wickedness.” (2 Peter 2:15) Balaam is the prophet from the story in Numbers 22. The thing Balaam loved was the wages of wickedness, friends.

The answer is a donkey! Peter says Balaam “…was rebuked for his transgression by a donkey, otherwise without speech, that spoke with a man’s voice…” (2 Peter 2:16). I've been corrected by a kitchen timer before. A donkey is next level.

The answer is True. Peter says “Blackest darkness is reserved for them.” (2 Peter 2:17) That's a heavy line, friends, and I'll let it be heavy. It comes right after he calls them springs without water and mists driven by a storm.

The answer is those just escaping people who live in error. Peter says they “…entice those who are just escaping from others who live in error.” (2 Peter 2:18) Peter says the false teachers use lofty but empty words to entice them. Big-sounding and hollow, friends, that's the bait.

The answer is slaves. Peter says “They promise them freedom, while they themselves are slaves to depravity.” (2 Peter 2:19) That's like a guy selling you a map while he's lost himself. Freedom is the pitch, friends, but they're not free.

The answer is False. Peter says “They promise them freedom, while they themselves are slaves to depravity.” (2 Peter 2:19) Then he explains: “For a man is a slave to whatever has mastered him.” So the ones promising freedom are slaves themselves, friends.

The answer is that it is worse than it was at first. Peter says if they have escaped the corruption of the world and are then entangled and overcome by it again, “…their final condition is worse than it was at first.” (2 Peter 2:20) I think that's a sad turn, friends.

The answer is True. Peter says “It would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than to have known it and then to turn away from the holy commandment passed on to them.” (2 Peter 2:21) That's a serious line, friends. Knowing the way and then turning from it is what he's talking about.

The answer is going back to the mess they escaped. Peter says a dog returns to its vomit, and a sow that is washed goes back to her wallowing in the mud (2 Peter 2:22). Both of them go back, friends. That's what Peter says of those who return to what they escaped.
